problem.title: Design a Thread-Safe Bounded Blocking Queue
problem.prompt: Design and implement a thread-safe Bounded Blocking Queue with put(element) and get() methods. When the queue is full, producer threads calling put() must block until space becomes available. When the queue is empty, consumer threads calling get() must block until an element is added.
requirements: Bounded capacity specified at construction time.
put(element): inserts element, blocking if full until space is available.
get(): retrieves and removes head element, blocking if empty until element is available.
Thread safety: safe under concurrent access by multiple producer and consumer threads.
FIFO ordering: elements are retrieved in the order they were inserted.
constraints: No busy-waiting / polling loops (while true sleep). Must use condition synchronization.
Prevent deadlocks between producers and consumers.

stages.learnerPrompt: What is the difference between a mutex lock and a condition variable? Why is a single mutex insufficient without condition variables?

referenceMaterial.summary: A mutex provides mutual exclusion (only one thread enters critical section). Condition variables allow threads to release the mutex and sleep until signaled that state has changed. We need two conditions: notEmpty (consumers wait on) and notFull (producers wait on).
tradeOffs: One lock + two condition variables: clean, thread-safe, prevents deadlocks.
Two locks (head lock & tail lock like Java LinkedBlockingQueue): allows simultaneous enqueue and dequeue, boosting concurrency at cost of complex state tracking.

stages.learnerPrompt: Sketch your class implementation with put and get. Why must condition checks use while loops instead of if statements?
Review the reference implementation with circular array and condition variables.

referenceMaterial.summary: Circular buffer backed by an array, guarded by a ReentrantLock with notFull and notEmpty Condition instances.
approachSteps: 1. State: array items, head index, tail index, count, capacity, lock, notFull condition, notEmpty condition.
2. put(item): lock.lock() -> while (count === capacity) notFull.await() -> items[tail] = item -> tail = (tail + 1) % capacity -> count++ -> notEmpty.signal() -> lock.unlock().
3. get(): lock.lock() -> while (count === 0) notEmpty.await() -> item = items[head] -> head = (head + 1) % capacity -> count-- -> notFull.signal() -> return item -> lock.unlock().
alternatives: Lock-free circular ring buffer (Disruptor pattern): uses atomic CAS (compare-and-swap) and memory barriers to achieve millions of ops/sec without mutex overhead.
Semaphore-based implementation: two counting semaphores for items and spaces, plus a binary semaphore for mutex.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why use 'while (count === capacity)' instead of 'if (count === capacity)'? Explain spurious wakeups.

tradeOffs: Spurious wakeups: OS threads can wake from await() without an explicit signal. Using a while loop re-checks the predicate after wakeup, guaranteeing safety.
Multiple waiters: If signal() wakes multiple threads or another producer acquires lock first, the queue might be full again by the time the thread acquires the lock. The while loop catches this.

stages.learnerPrompt: Thread starvation: What happens if 100 producer threads are constantly waiting to insert and consumers process slowly? How does a fair lock vs non-fair lock impact latency and throughput?

failureModes: Thread starvation with non-fair locks: Newly arrived threads can steal the lock from waiting threads, causing long-tail latency for waiting threads.
Fair Lock (FIFO acquisition): Guarantees no thread starves, but throughput drops significantly (up to 4x slower) due to context switches.
SignalAll thundering herd: Calling signalAll() wakes all waiting threads, but only one acquires the lock while the rest sleep again. Always use signal() unless broadcasting a state reset.

stages.learnerPrompt: Follow-up: How would you add a timeout to put (e.g. put(item, timeoutMillis)) to prevent indefinite producer blocking?

approachSteps: 1. Use condition.awaitNanos(nanosTimeout) inside the while loop.
3. If nanosTimeout <= 0 and count === capacity, return false (timed out).
tradeOffs: Timeout protection: Prevents resource deadlock in microservices when downstream consumers freeze.
